  SUBJECT:  CONSOLIDATED ANNUAL PERFORMANCE AND EVALUATION REPORT (CAPER)
  FOR FY 2020-21

  Recommendation:

  Staff recommends that the City Council conduct a public hearing and take public testimony on the City’s FY 2020-
  21 Consolidated Annual Performance and Evaluation Report. No further City Council action is necessary.

  Background:

  The City of Lynwood's Community Development Department has completed its Consolidated Annual
  Performance and Evaluation Report (CAPER) for the period July 1, 2020 through June 30, 2021. The CAPER
  describes the overall use of federal Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) and HOME Investment
  Partnerships (HOME) funds received from the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) in
  relationship to the needs of the community as outlined in its FY 2020-21 Annual Action Plan. The City’s overall
  objective in the CDBG and HOME programs is the development of viable communities by providing decent
  housing, a suitable living environment, and expansion of economic opportunities primarily for low-to-moderate
  income persons.

  Discussion and Analysis:

  The City submits a CAPER to HUD annually as one of the conditions of receiving federal funds under the CDBG
  and HOME programs. The CAPER outlines progress made in achieving goals established in the City’s Five-
  Year Consolidated Plan and Annual Action Plan, including: 1) funds invested in projects and activities; 2)
  households and persons assisted; 3) actions taken to affirmatively further fair housing; and 4) other information
  relevant to grant-funded projects administered by the City that affect local housing and community development
  needs. The CAPER is an effective tool, designed to ensure the City stays on track with its Five-Year
  Consolidated Plan and Annual Action Plan. The CAPER is also designed to provide a maximum amount of
  useful information to policy makers and residents.

  During FY 2020-21, the City spent $2,511,306 of CDBG funds and $302,871 of HOME funds on a variety of

  The City has continuously sought public and private resources to leverage its entitlement funds
  in assisting with implementation of policies and programs to implement the Consolidated Plan.

  Federal Resources and Program Funds Used - It is the City's goal to maximize use of available
  resources by committing to projects that are financially feasible and assist the greatest number
  of people and families. To this end, two resources were utilized during the FY 2020-21: the
  CDBG Program and the HOME Program.

  AGENDA STAFF REPORT

  DATE:  October 19, 2021

  TO:  Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council

  APPROVED BY: Ernie Hernandez, City Manager

  SUBJECT:  APPROVAL OF AT&T CALNET NEXTGEN CONTRACT

  Recommendation:

  Staff recommends that the City Council adopt the attached resolution entitled; “A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY
  COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF LYNWOOD AUTHORIZING THE MAYOR OR DESIGNEE TO ENTER INTO
  AN AGREEMENT WITH AT&T AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER TO SIGN CONTRACTS W ITH AT&T TO
  PROVIDE TELECOMMUNICATION SERVICES TO THE CITY OF LYNW OOD THROUGH THE STATE OF
  CALIFORNIA NEGOTIATED CONTRACT KNOW N AS CALNET NEXTGEN."

  Background:

  The California Department of Technology has been competitively bidding on telecommunication services through
  state awarded contracts known as the California Network and Telecommunication (CALNET) program since
  1998. The City of Lynwood has been piggy-backing on this contract since 2002 moving from CALNET to CALNET 2,
  then CALNET 3 to take advantage of the discounted pricing for telecommunication services.

  Discussion and Analysis:

  The State’s CALNET 3 is set to expire on December 31, 2021. The State went out to bid to establish a new
  contract to replace the expiring agreement and awarded AT&T the contract to provide phone and data line
  services, referred to as CALNET NextGen. CALNET NextGen is a five year contract and offers a wide variety of
  services, including long distance, trunk lines, internet, fiber optic, data lines, and wireless lines at discounted rates.

  The City of Lynwood can take advantage of the discounted pricing by participating in the cooperative agreement
  and contracting with AT&T through the CALNET NextGen contract. This contract stipulates that the City remain
  under contract for five years.

  If the City does not participate in the cooperative agreement, the phone and data line services will be charged at
  the tariff rate, which is about 20-30% higher than the CALNET NextGen rate. To maintain a competitive rate, the
  City must then develop an RFP and bid for these services. This will require the City to develop and evaluate all

City Council Regular Meeting - Page 88 of 171
   plans under consideration, and it is unlikely these plans would realize the cost savings the CALNET NextGen
  contract offers. Since the City will realize a reduction in costs associated with the CALNET NextGen contract,
  staff recommends participating in the cooperative agreement by authorizing the City Manager to sign the
  CALNET NextGen contracts on behalf of the City:
  Attachment 1 - CalNet 19.1 ATO form
  Attachment 2 - CalNet DNCS form
  Attachment 3 - CalNet Legacy ATO form
  Attachment 4 - CalNet Ordering forms
  Attachment 5 - Non E-Rate Rider form

  Lynwood Municipal Code § 6-3.9 requires that professional service contracts exceeding $25,000.00 must be
  procured via an RFP process unless the Council finds that the contract approval is exempt for the RFP process
  pursuant to LMC § 6-3.13.

  Accordingly, approval of the AT&T CalNet NextGen agreement requires a City Council vote of 4/5 of the
  members. Since the State of California competitively bid on these services, it would be more economical and
  efficient for the City to use this contract.

  Fiscal Impact:

  Staff budgeted $75,000 for telephone landline and wireless services for Fiscal Year 2021-2022. $75,000 was
  budgeted for telephone landline and wireless servicdes for Fiscal Year 2022-2023.

  In order to stay within the budget by taking advantage of competitively pre-bid rates by the State of California, staff
  requests approval of this item.

  Recommendation:

  Staff recommends that the City Council adopt the attached resolution entitled: “A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY
  COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF LYNWOOD ACCEPTING THE SANBORN AVENUE AND MULFORD
  AVENUE PARKING LOTS IMPROVEMENT PROJECT (CIP NO. 4011.68.081) AS COMPLETE;
  AUTHORIZING THE FILING OF THE NOTICE OF COMPLETION WITH THE LOS ANGELES COUNTY
  RECORDER’S OFFICE AND THE RELEASE OF THE 5% RETENTION 35 DAYS AFTER THE
  ACCEPTANCE.”

  Background:

  On March 24, 2020, the Notice Inviting Bids for the project was advertised in the Daily Journal, Bid America, on
  the City’s web site (PlanetBids). The bid opening took place in the PlanetBids Platform on Thursday, April 9,
  2020 at 10:00 A.M. (Pacific Time).

  Project Scope

  The Sanborn Avenue and Mulford Avenue Parking Lots Improvement Project consists of parking lot resurfacing,
  and partial replacement of concrete sidewalks, traffic signing and striping, installation of lights, pullboxes, conduit,
  service meters, landscaping and irrigation.

  Project Limit

  Sanborn Avenue and Mulford Avenue Parking lots are located between Long Beach Blvd and California Avenue.

City Council Regular Meeting - Page 108 of 171
   Discussion and Analysis:

  On April 21, 2020, the City awarded the contract to the lowest responsible bidder, Aramexx Group, Inc., in the
  amount of $326,434.80 for the construction of the Project.

  The construction on of the Project started on June 9, 2020. The final inspection and substantial project completion
  was on August 31, 2020. The project had significant delays due to Edison plan review. Because this was a long
  lead time, City decided to remove the Installation of Light poles and energizing of cabinets from existing contract
  and create a Phase 2 to avoid additional delays to the contract. Staff conducted the final inspection for phase 1 of
  the project and found that all work was completed in accordance with the project plans and specifications.

  Approved Budget

  A budget of $490,537 was approved by the City Council in FY20. The funding source approved was from the
  Lease Revenue Bond (Fund 9053).

  The Project budget balance from FY21 is being carried over to FY22 to undertake the recommended Phase 2
  activities relation to the light poles and energizing of the cabinets.

  Change Orders

  On April 21, 2020, the City Council authorized the City Manager under LMC 6-3.15(d) to exceed the specific
  dollar amounts or percentage limitations under LMC 6-3.15(a) and authorized the City Manager to approve
  consultant, vendor agreements, modifications, change orders or agreement amendments related to the Project up
  to the available Project Budgets. (Resolution 2020.053)

  In compliance with LMC 6-3.15(f) which requires the City Manager to report to the City Council every three months
  or with the project acceptance report on modifications and change orders, staff is reporting on the modifications
  and change orders approved by the City Manager as part of this project acceptance agenda item.

  The City Manager approved six (6) contract change orders for the total amount of $24,378.50 (See attachment A).

  The Project is now ready for acceptance by the City Council. Once accepted, staff can record the Notice of
  Completion at the County Recorder’s Office. Staff will then release retention 35 days after the project acceptance.

  No additional funding is needed

  Recommendation:

  Staff recommends that the City Council adopt the following resolution entitled: “A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY
  COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF LYNWOOD AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER OR HIS DESIGNEE TO
  APPLY FOR THE U.S. BUREAU OF RECLAMATION 2021 WATERSMART GRANT FOR AMI DATA
  COLLECTION SYSTEM AND AMRI METERS.”

  Background:

  Through WaterSMART Water and Energy Efficiency Grants (formerly Challenge Grants) the U.S. Bureau of
  Reclamation provides 50/50 cost share funding to irrigation and water districts, tribes, states and other entities
  with water or power delivery authority. Eligible projects include those projects that conserve and use water more
  efficiently; increase the production of hydropower; mitigate conflict risk in areas at a high risk of future water
  conflict; and accomplish other benefits that contribute to water supply reliability in the western United States.
  Projects are selected through a competitive process and the focus is on projects that can be completed within two
  or three years.

  Discussion and Analysis:

  By using Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) meters or smart meters, the City would receive several benefits.
  The AMI meters are more accurate than the current displacement type water meters therefore obtaining the full
  value of water sold to residents and businesses. The use of AMI meters would reduce the labor required to obtain
  meter reads for billing and those staff hours to be redirected to other crucial water operations. Remote meter
  reading would eliminate the need to access the meters which could be located in difficult locations. The benefits
  for residents and businesses would include: improved billing accuracy, elimination of misreads or inaccurate
  readings, obtaining information about water consumption patterns which might help diagnose problems leading to
  high utility bills, assistance in detecting leaks earlier allowing for preventative maintenance, and helping customers

City Council Regular Meeting - Page 114 of 171
   manage their consumption to help meet water conservation goals.

  According to SAFNA, the City’s utility consultant, the average accuracy of current water meters is 91.84%
  translating into an estimated annual revenue loss of $518,700 annually. The estimate for operational cost savings
  which includes personnel costs equate to $9.8 million over the next 20 years.

  In FY21, the City Council adopted a budget of $1,307,286 for the Advanced Metering Infrastructure (CIP No.
  4011.67.070). During the budget process for FY22, staff estimated FY21 year-end estimate at $736,286,
  however, actual expenditure for FY21 was $5,000. Staff was not able to purchase the smart meters in FY21as
  anticipated. Since CIP projects are often completed within multiple fiscal years, when necessary, staff returns
  back to the City Council to reconcile the difference between the actual expenditure and estimated year end
  expenditure to ensure that the unused funds are carried over to the following fiscal year and the project remains
  fully funded. This process is referred to as “true up” process.

  The table below shows the City Council adopted projects related to the smart meters purchase and installation as
  included in the FY21-22 and FY22-23 Adopted Biennial Budget.

  Program) is distributed among nine watershed areas, to be programmed by the respective Watershed Area
  Steering Committees. The percentage of funds received by each Watershed Area is proportional to the tax
  revenues collected within its boundaries.
  On September 15, 2021, the Los Angeles County Flood Control District (County) Governing Body approved the
  recommended Stormwater Investment Plans (SIPs) for Fiscal Year 2021-22 (FY22) for the Safe Clean Water
  Program’s Regional Program. Included in the Lower Los Angeles River Watershed SIP is a project from the City
  entitled Lynwood City Park Stormwater Capture Project (Project). The Project is to develop a regional stormwater
  capture infiltration system that will also install a new parking lot, soccer field and ephemeral stream at the Lynwood
  City Park. The Safe, Clean Water grant funding is $1,691,629 to fund the environmental planning, permitting,

  Discussion and Analysis:

  Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System (MS4) receive stormwater and non-stormwater discharges from
  various sources, including municipal MS4s and other public agencies, discharges under the NPDES permits or
  authorized by the USEPA, groundwater and natural flow. As the discharges flow over the urban landscape, they
  may pick up pollutants generated by urban activities, such as metals, bacteria, pesticides, fertilizers and trash.
  Polluted stormwater and non-stornwater discharges conveyed through the MS4 ultimately reach receiving waters,
  resulting in adverse water quality impacts. The goal of the MS4 Permit is to reduce the discharge of these
  pollutants from MS4.

  To comply with the MS4 Permit, the City joined the Lower Los Angeles River Watershed Group (LLAR Group) to
  jointly undertake certain MS4 permit requirements at a watershed level. The LLAR Group under which the City is
  a member commissioned a study and infiltration testing to develop a stormwater project in Lynwood that would
  help the watershed comply with MS4 Permit.

  The Safe, Clean Water Program provides funding for stormwater projects under a competitive call for projects. To
  supplement the City’s resources, staff submitted a grant application to obtain grant funding for the Lynwood City
  Park Stormwater Capture Project. The Project is to develop a regional stormwater capture and infiltration system
  that will also install a new parking lot, soccer filed and ephemeral stream at Lynwood City Park. The grant funding
  obtained successfully was for $1,691,629 to fund the environmental planning, permitting, design, and community
  outreach and project management. Once the design phase is completed, staff will seek out funding for

   EXHIBIT E – NATURE BASED SOLUTIONS (NBS) BEST MANAGEMENT
  PRACTICES

  Nature-based solutions (NBS) refers to the sustainable management and use of nature
  for undertaking socio-environmental challenges, including climate change, water security,
  water pollution, food security, human health, and disaster risk management. As this
  environmental management practice is increasingly incorporated into projects for the
  SCW Program, this guidance document may be expanded upon to further quantify NBS
  practices based on benefits derived from their incorporation on projects.
  The SCW Program defines NBS as a Project that utilizes natural processes that slow,
  detain, infiltrate or filter Stormwater or Urban Runoff. These methods may include relying
  predominantly on soils and vegetation; increasing the permeability of Impermeable Areas;
  protecting undeveloped mountains and floodplains; creating and restoring riparian habitat
  and wetlands; creating rain gardens, bioswales, and parkway basins; enhancing soil
  through composting, mulching; and, planting trees and vegetation, with preference for
  native species. NBS may also be designed to provide additional benefits such as
  sequestering carbon, supporting biodiversity, providing shade, creating and enhancing
  parks and open space, and improving quality of life for surrounding communities. NBS
  include Projects that mimic natural processes, such as green streets, spreading grounds
  and planted areas with water storage capacity. NBS may improve water quality, collect
  water for reuse or aquifer recharge, or to support vegetation growth utilizing natural
  processes.
  Recipients are to consider using Nature-Based Solutions for infrastructure projects and
  include in each Quarterly Progress/Expenditure Report and annual summary whether and
  how their project achieves a good, better, or best for each of the 6 NBS methods in
  accordance with the guidance below. Additionally, Quarterly Progress/Expenditure
  Reports should include discussion on any considerations taken to maximize the class
  within each method. If at least 3 methods score within a single class, the overall project
  can be characterized as that class. Recipients must attach a copy of the matrix for each
  Project with the good, better, or best column indicated for each method, to facilitate
  District tracking of methods being utilized.

  Recipient or approved Project operator shall operate and maintain infrastructure projects
  for the useful life of the project and are to consider using the following guidance for
  operations and maintenance. Operational maintenance is the care and upkeep of Projects
  that may require detailed technical knowledge of the Project’s function and design. Project
  specific operational and maintenance plans shall consider the activities listed below and
  set forth specific activities and frequencies (not limited to those below) as determined to
  be appropriate by the Municipalities and best practices, including stakeholder
  engagement as applicable. Operational maintenance is to be performed by the operator
  of the Project with a purpose to make the operator aware of the state of readiness of the
  Project to deliver stormwater and urban runoff benefits.

  1.  Litter Control
  • Regularly removal of litter, nonhazardous waste materials, and
  accumulated debris near planted areas, rock areas, decomposed granite
  areas, rest areas, fence perimeters, adjoining access roads and driveways,
  drains, pedestrian trails, viewing stations, shelter houses, and bicycle
  pathways.
  • Regularly inspection and maintenance of pet waste stations
  • Maintaining trash receptacles
  • Removal of trash, debris, and blockages from bioswales
  • Inspection and cleaning of trash booms
  • Inspection of weir gates and stop logs to clean debris, as required.

  o Recognition and removal of weeds, such as perennial weeds,
  morning glory, vine-type weeds, ragweed, and other underground
  spreading weeds.
  o Avoiding activities that result in weed seed germination (e.g. frequent
  soil cultivation near trees or shrubs)
  o Regularly removal of weeds from landscape areas, including from
  berms, painted areas, rock areas, gravel areas, pavement cracks
  along access roads and driveways, drains, pedestrian trails, viewing
  stations, park shelters, and bicycle paths.

  o Prevent encroachment of adjacent property and provide vertical

  o Inspect for dead or diseased plants regularly

  o Installation and maintenance of hydrophytic and emergent plants in
